sources.news_title: Tennessee Democrat unseats one of the grossest members of Congress
sources.text:
Democrat Victoria Broderick just flipped a deep-red seat in Tennessee’s 4th District, with The Associated Press officially calling the race on Tuesday. It’s one of the most shocking upsets of the midterms.
Broderick defeated GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais, whose district President Donald Trump won by 24 points in 2024.
The district was not considered competitive by any of the race-rating organizations; even data-based election models like FiftyPlusOne rated the race as safe for the GOP. There wasn’t any polling to indicate that this race was even in the realm of being competitive.
Indeed, Broderick—who lost to DesJarlais in 2024 by more than 43 points—spent just $90,000 in her rematch, according to Federal Election Commission records. And none of that money went toward television ads.
But in wave years like 2026, there are often shocking winners, where incumbents of the party in the White House lose in races that no one saw coming. This year, that was DesJarlais.
His ouster is both satisfying and deeply poetic.
A physician by trade, DesJarlais was swept into Congress in the 2010 red wave, when he defeated incumbent Democratic Rep. Lincoln Davis. DesJarlais won even though his abhorrent personal conduct—including physical abuse allegations—went public.
After he was elected, even more disturbing behavior from DesJarlais’ past came out, including multiple affairs with patients from his medical practice—leading to fines from a medical board.
And DesJarlais, who claimed to be against abortion, had pressured his now-ex-wife to get multiple abortions.
Disgusted by DesJarlais’ conduct and hypocrisy, Republicans tried to rid themselves of him in the 2014 cycle. They ran a top-tier candidate against him in a primary, and made DesJarlais’ personal transgressions part of that campaign.
But DesJarlais survived by the skin of his teeth, winning renomination by just 35 votes—with a splintered GOP primary field boosting him to victory.
Related | Republicans work feverishly to save 2 deep-red House seats
After that, Republicans gave up on trying to oust him, and he served for 12 more years as a backbencher who introduced just 52 bills in his 16 years in office—not a single one of which became law.
But more than a decade later, a Democrat pulled off what Republicans never could. With Broderick’s win, Democrats will now hold at least 259 seats in the incoming Congress—the largest number either party has had in the chamber since 1993.
Democrats also lead in Minnesota’s 1st District—which is currently heading to a recount. That would give Democrats 260 seats.
There are also two runoffs on Dec. 12 in Louisiana, where Democrats are unlikely to win. But Broderick has proven that surprises can happen.

sources.news_title: Democrats Reach 259 House Seats as Jeffries Promises Trump Probes
sources.text:
House Democrats secured at least 259 seats in the next Congress on Tuesday, after Democrat Victoria Broderick unseated Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-TN) in Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District.
Republicans will hold no fewer than 173 seats, with three races still uncalled, the Associated Press (AP) reported. The tally is the Democrat party’s best election result since 1990.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) claimed on election night that voters had turned on Republican rule.
“Today begins the great American comeback,” the Brooklyn Democrat said.
Democrats gained 45 seats from where they started on Election Day, five more than the 40 they picked up in 2018. Their majority tops the 258 seats won after Bill Clinton’s 1992 election and the 257 won with Barack Obama in 2008.
Party leaders have said they will open the term with health care and cost-of-living votes, then turn their committees on the administration. Jeffries told ABC’s This Week in September that Democrats had ruled nothing in or out on impeachment, and he named Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) to run accountability work at the Judiciary Committee.
The incoming Speaker has already backed one impeachment push.
“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” he said of the measure targeting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which was written by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY).
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), who is bidding to run the Oversight Committee, argued that Stephen Miller’s immigration work warrants investigation, and he wants Elon Musk questioned over DOGE’s handling of personal data.
The White House warned Democrats over the planned probes and suggested some of them could amount to criminality. Attorney General Todd Blanche said his department was prepared to respond and could investigate Democrat lawmakers over threatening rhetoric.
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) wrote after the election that the new majority would be run by “the most radical and extreme leftists in American history.”
Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) was elected Republican leader for the minority. “Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said.
DesJarlais lost the seat after eight terms. Broderick carried two of the district’s 11 counties and finished roughly 280 votes ahead, and the Tennessee Republican said he had “personally reached out to Ms. Broderick” to congratulate her.
Minnesota’s 1st District goes to a recount beginning Nov. 30, and Louisiana’s 5th and 6th Districts head to runoffs on Dec. 12, Yahoo News reported.
Senate Democrats, who will hold 56 seats, pick a leader on Dec. 1. Trump posted that it would be “very hard” for him to work with Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) if Schumer takes the job.

The road to 259
The latest House win to be certified is one of the least likely:
Democrats picked up their 259th seat in the House on Tuesday, as their victory in a largely rural district in Tennessee gave them their largest majority in three decades.
Victoria Broderick, a progressive tech support worker who ran for the House as a Democrat, narrowly defeated Representative Scott DesJarlais, according to The Associated Press, unseating an eight-term Republican in one of the biggest upsets this cycle.
Her victory in Tennessee’s Fourth Congressional District will give the Democrats their biggest majority since the early 1990s, when the party held 267 seats. In the largest House majority on record, Democrats won 334 seats in 1936. Republicans won their largest House majority, 302 seats, in 1920.
“Whether you voted for me or not, I want you to know that I will be your representative,” Ms. Broderick said in a statement Tuesday. “I look forward to listening and doing the work you’ve entrusted me to do.”
A few House races were not yet called as of Tuesday, including Minnesota’s First District, which will advance to a recount on Nov. 30, and Louisiana’s Fifth and Sixth Districts, where runoff elections are scheduled in December. In all three districts, which Mr. Trump won, Democrats were leading overall by a slim margin.
Ms. Broderick’s victory was one of the most striking upsets by Democrats in the midterms in part because many election forecasters had rated her race as solidly Republican. President Trump had won the Fourth District by 24 points in 2024, making it the constituency most strongly aligned with Mr. Trump that Democrats have taken so far. And Mr. DesJarlais defeated Ms. Broderick by 43 points just two years ago.
She had also been outspent by a vast margin. Her campaign spent just over $90,000, compared with $508,000 spent by Mr. DesJarlais, according to Federal Election Commission data. Her campaign had no record of airing a television ad.
One of my few regrets about the midterms is that Justin Pearson wasn’t able to beat the racial gerrymander in TN-9, losing by a little more than a point. But this is at least a little compensation. Her reason for getting into the race is compelling:
Ms. Broderick, 34, was born in Brandon, Fla., and lived in several places in the South, including in San Antonio and Atlanta, before her family moved to Tennessee in 2007, she said in an interview. She said she was involved with the Democratic Party in high school, but her experience of a miscarriage in 2021 helped deepen her political activism.
The failure of her intrauterine device, or IUD, led her to discover that she was pregnant, she said. Ms. Broderick had to navigate the medical care system, and then miscarried, which she described as an education in the physical challenges of a pregnancy.
About a month later, she said, she became pregnant again. While she was on maternity leave after having her baby, the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. That decision, she said, compelled her to act.
“I can’t stand by anymore,” she recalled thinking. “I have to do more.”
She will not be the last woman motivated to get into politics by Dobbs, and good.

sources.news_title: Tennessee’s Victoria Broderick becomes the first pansexual person elected to U.S. Congress
sources.text:
Her Republican opponent conceded more than a week ago, but the Associated Press officially declared Victoria Broderick the winner of rural Tennessee’s 4th congressional district on Tuesday, making her the 259th Democrat elected to the House of Representatives in this month's historic midterm “blue wave.”
In addition to securing the largest House majority for either party since 1992, Broderick also sets another key precedent: She is the first openly pansexual person elected to U.S. Congress.
Broderick, 34, is a married mother of two boys who worked in tech support and won her race without purchasing a single television ad. When she is sworn-in come January, it appears that Broderick will be not only the first out pansexual member of Congress, but the first pansexual elected to any national office.
Broderick revealed she identifies as pansexual in an interview with Nashville's NPR station earlier this month, also telling WPLN News that she supports the “T” in LGBTQ+.
Related: Lawmaker: I'm Not a Lesbian, I'm Pansexual
“Trans people aren’t the reason your gas and grocery prices are getting more expensive,” Broderick said. “Any politician talking about the trans community is lazy. They’re lazy, and they are neglecting answering real questions and actually addressing the issues.”
A spokesperson for the Human Rights Campaign called her "a history maker" in a statement for The Advocate.
“Congresswoman-elect Broderick is a history-maker not just because of who she is, but because of the kind of campaign she ran," HRC director of communications Laurel Powell said. "She refused to throw any community under the bus or walk back her principles. Instead, she showed you can win just about anywhere, against just about anyone, if you stay true to who you are and prove you can deliver for families of all backgrounds. We look forward to working with her and every other history-maker in the new Congress.”
Broderick joins a small group of pansexual Americans elected to public office, two of whom are still serving in Texas and California. Mary Gonzalez serves in the statehouse of the Lone Star State and in 2012 became America's first out pansexual elected. Terra Lawson-Remer still serves as the county supervisor in San Diego. Sarah Peters was elected to the Nevada Assembly in 2018, and her term ended in 2024.
Related: 27 groundbreaking LGBTQ+ politicians & public officials who are moving equality forward
As The New York Times reported, Broderick squeaked to victory on fewer than 400 votes and unseated an eight-term Republican, Rep. Scott DesJarlais. Tennessee law does not allow for recounts.
Related: Chief Justice-elect Maggie Ellis becomes first LGBTQ+ person in Texas to win statewide race
Broderick lost to DesJarlais two years ago and said she won this time by pressing her message on social media, posting campaign videos that won her votes from Republicans and Independents as well as Democrats.
“Whether you voted for me or not, I want you to know that I will be your representative,” Broderick said in a statement Tuesday. “I look forward to listening and doing the work you’ve entrusted me to do.”
The Advocate reached out to Broderick's campaign for comment but did not receive a response as of press time.

sources.news_title: Democrat flips Tennessee House seat in major upset
Democrat Victoria Broderick Flips GOP House Seat in Tennessee
sources.text:
PIKEVILLE, Tenn.—Democrat Victoria Broderick has unseated Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.) and flipped a Tennessee House seat that Republicans had held since 2011.
Broderick has led in the Tennessee Secretary of State’s unofficial results since election night and declared victory the next day. DesJarlais conceded on Nov. 16, and The Associated Press called the race for Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District on Nov. 24. The state expects to certify the results on Dec. 1, according to the secretary of state’s office.
Broderick won 95,585 votes, or 48.87 percent, to DesJarlais’s 95,305, or 48.73 percent, a margin of 280 votes.
“I am honored and humbled that the people of Tennessee’s 4th District have voted to send a working-class mom from Lincoln to represent them in the halls of Congress,” Broderick said in her post declaring victory.
“Our victory is a shared victory for every Tennessean who is tired of the corruption in Washington that is costing all of us, from Davidson to Rutherford and everywhere in between.”
Her lead in the secretary of state’s unofficial results had remained at fewer than 300 votes since election night. DesJarlais held off on conceding while about 700 provisional ballots were still uncounted, most of them in Nashville. He conceded after the Davidson County Election Commission counted its share. Tennessee does not have an automatic recount.
“I have personally reached out to Ms. Broderick to offer my congratulations and my support on this new undertaking,” DesJarlais wrote on Facebook, saying his campaign had come “just a few hundred votes short out of just under 200,000 votes cast.”
“All of us hope that the new Member of Congress feels the same level of awe and gratitude for this tremendous undertaking that I felt every day I had the privilege of serving,” he added.
“To everything, there is a season, and I will leave here with great love and affection for my time in the Congress, thankful for all of the friends made, and very much looking forward to the next chapter of my life.”
Broderick, 34, is a tech support worker from Fayetteville and a former Lincoln County Democratic Party chair. She campaigned on affordability. DesJarlais beat her in 2024 with 70 percent of the vote.
Before this year’s election, Tennessee Republicans redrew the state’s congressional map. The new map added part of Nashville to the 4th District and split Memphis among three districts. Broderick carried only two of the district’s 11 counties, Davidson and Rutherford, which are its two most populous.
Broderick will be the only Democrat in Tennessee’s nine-member House delegation. Republicans won the other eight seats, including all three districts that now divide Memphis.
In the governor’s race, Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) defeated Democrat Jerri Green.

sources.text:
Democrat Victoria Broderick defeated eight-term Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District by a margin of fewer than 400 votes, The Associated Press projected on Tuesday.
Broderick’s victory aids Democrats’ nearly record-high House majority and marks the 48th House seat flip for Democrats this cycle.
The Democrat had declared victory in a social media post two days after Election Day and attended freshman orientation events in Washington, D.C., this month. DesJarlais conceded Nov. 16 in a post on Facebook, saying he “personally reached out” to Broderick to congratulate her.
Broderick’s win in a “solid R” district that President Donald Trump carried by 24 percentage points in 2024 represents a massive upset for the Republican Party. DesJarlais significantly outraised and outspent Broderick, with the Republican raising more than $660,000 and the Democrat bringing in less than $100,000, according to financial disclosures.
Trending
The same factors in Democrats’ nationwide success, including high prices, probably contributed to Broderick’s win, but she told the Nashville Banner that she never truly stopped campaigning after losing to DesJarlais by more than 40 points in 2024.
Tennessee’s redistricting push also may have helped Broderick win her race, after the Republican-led general assembly redrew the state’s congressional maps this year in a successful effort to push longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen out of his seat.
Even though Republicans held an apparent advantage in all nine of Tennessee’s seats heading into Election Day, the redistricting push gave the 4th District parts of Nashville’s Democratic stronghold in Davidson County. Under the new map, residents in Broderick’s district are about 20 points less Republican, according to an analysis by Inside Elections.

“Democrats picked up their 259th seat in the House on Tuesday, as their victory in a largely rural district in Tennessee gave them their largest majority in three decades,” the New York Times reports.
“Victoria Broderick, a progressive tech support worker who ran for the House as a Democrat, narrowly defeated Representative Scott DesJarlais, according to The Associated Press, unseating an eight-term Republican in one of the biggest upsets this cycle.”

sources.news_title: Victoria Broderick defeats Tennessee Rep. Scott DesJarlais
sources.text:
Democrat knocks off Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee
Victoria Broderick flips deep-red seat in one of party’s most unexpected midterm wins
Democrat Victoria Broderick, seen here speaking to a reporter outside the Capitol on Nov. 11, has unseated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)
Democrat Victoria Broderick has defeated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee’s 4th District, giving her party the 259th seat of its commanding House majority in the next Congress.
Broderick, a tech support worker, was leading by 361 votes when The Associated Press called the race Tuesday, three weeks after all votes were cast.
Broderick’s victory ranks among the most surprising Democratic wins of this year’s midterm elections. DesJarlais, who defeated Broderick in 2024 by more than 40 points, was not considered vulnerable heading into Election Day.
But the election two years ago took place under a previous version of Tennessee’s congressional map. Following this spring’s Supreme Court ruling that limited the use of race in redistricting, the state’s Republican-led legislature redrew the House lines to eliminate Rep. Steve Cohen’s Memphis-area district, the lone seat held by Democrats.
In doing so, though, the new map significantly altered the boundaries of the largely rural 4th District in Middle Tennessee, which now extends into Nashville’s Davidson County. Thirty-three percent of DesJarlais’ constituents were new to him, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, as the district shifted from one that Donald Trump carried by 43 points in 2024 to one that would have backed him by 24 points.
Under the new map, Republicans struggled to win most of the state’s House seats earlier this month. They narrowly won Cohen’s 9th District, one of just three flips for the party this year nationwide. But Broderick’s win ensures that Tennessee will continue to have a Democrat in its congressional delegation.
DesJarlais had already conceded the race before Tuesday’s AP call.
“As the final votes have now been tabulated in this new and completely restructured district, it appears that we have a result showing my campaign has come just a few hundred votes short out of just under 200,000 votes cast,” he said in a Nov. 16 statement congratulating Broderick.
A member of the hard-line conservative Freedom Caucus, DesJarlais was first elected in 2010, unseating Democrat Lincoln Davis. While he’d been comfortably reelected in the years since, he faced competitive primaries in 2014 and 2016 after his divorce records came to light.
Broderick, a mother of two and a former chair of the Lincoln County Democratic Party, raised less than $100,000 for her campaign, compared with more than $650,000 for DesJarlais. She also defeated a better-funded opponent in the Democratic primary.
She told PBS NewsHour that she had essentially been campaigning for the seat since launching her 2024 bid and built relationships across the district that helped her win.
“I never stopped running for Congress. And when it was redistricted, I just essentially said, well, the district stayed the same and actually became more competitive,” she said. “So the work's going to start speaking for itself real soon. And we saw that happen.”
Three House races remain uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon. Louisiana will hold runoffs in December for two districts, including a Democrat-held seat that Republicans redrew in their favor. The race for Minnesota’s 1st District is heading for a hand recount, with Republican Rep. Brad Finstad trailing Democratic challenger Jake Johnson by 324 votes.

sources.news_title: Victoria Broderick officially wins Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District, per AP
sources.text:
Victoria Broderick officially wins Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District, per AP
TENNESSEE (WZTV) — Democratic candidate Victoria Broderick has won Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District after The Associated Press called the race at 11:12 am CDT on Tuesday.
Broderick was projected to defeat Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais and independent candidates Jacob Kristopher Anders and Clay Faircloth.
RELATED COVERAGE | Nashville in Focus: Tennessee governor's race, the numbers you should notice
Broderick will represent communities in Bledsoe, Cannon, Coffee, Davidson, Franklin, Grundy, Marion, Rutherford, Sequatchie, Van Buren and Warren counties. She is a technology and logistics professional from Fayetteville and previously ran for the seat in 2024.
During the campaign, Broderick emphasized affordability, health care access, support for rural hospitals, housing and voluntary pre-K.

sources.news_title: Democrat flips Tennessee House Seat in one of biggest 2026 upsets
sources.text:
Democrat Victoria Broderick was elected to the U.S. House from Tennessee, narrowly defeating Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais after GOP redistricting made the district slightly more competitive.
Broderick’s upset victory further pads Democrats’ House majority, their largest since 1992, which now stands at 259 seats with one race still too early to call and two others going to runoffs next month.
DesJarlais is a physician who was first elected to the House in 2010. The race was a rematch against Broderick, whom he defeated in 2024 with a whopping 70% of the vote. But Republican state lawmakers narrowed the GOP’s overwhelming advantage in the district when they redrew the boundaries in an effort to pick up a Democratic-held seat in Memphis, which was successful.
The Associated Press called the Tennessee race on Tuesday with Broderick leading DesJarlais by fewer than 400 votes out of about 196,000, a margin of 0.18 percentage points.
The race in Minnesota’s 1st District is the last uncalled House contest. Democratic challenger Jake Johnson leads Republican Rep. Brad Finstad by 0.1 points, and a recount is scheduled to begin on Nov. 30.
Two races in Louisiana will be decided in a December runoff.
